newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end higher but volumes lower.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end higher but volumes lower.

text.p: New York precious metals futures ended slightly higher Wednesday, but volumes were lower than in recent sessions, as the market took a breather after heavy falls in the first two weeks of the year.

"There was some light fund shortcovering and some attempt to spark a rally near the close, but the trade and funds then sold into it again," Credit Lyonnais Rouse New York chief dealer, Scott Mehlman, said.
"With the Dutch central bank sale behind the market and Bundesbank president Tietmeyer pledging no more immediate sales, gold may start to form a base near $350," he said.
But the US dollar and stockmarket remained strong, providing little incentive for gold investment, traders said.

COMEX February gold ended up $1.80 an ounce at $355.00, as the contract consolidated after seeing a fresh contract lows Wednesday at $352.60. Total estimated volume was 35,000 lots, compared with 53,125 lots Wednesday.

In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $354.10/60, compared to the London Thursday afternoon fix at $353.05 and the New York close Wednesday at $352.25/75. Spot gold saw a fresh three year low Wednesday at $352.45.

"Despite the fact that other European central banks are not likely to sell gold in the immediate future, market participants remain nervous about possible central bank activity," CPM Group analyst Jeffrey Christian said.

While European central banks may be expected to sell gold in the future, they are unlikely to do so to help their governments meet the fiscal and debt-to-GDP ratios necessary for participation in European Monetary Union (EMU) under the Maastricht Treaty, Christian argued.

"The fact is the total amount of gold held by most EU central banks is minuscule compared to the financial requirements these governments face as they seek to qualify for entry into the first round of monetary union," he said.

The rules for EMU qualification include a 1997 government budget deficit not exceeding three percent of GDP and a government debt not exceeding 60 pct of GDP, but few European countries meet these criteria.
On Monday the Dutch central bank said it sold 300 tonnes of gold, about one fifth of its reserves, and an amount equivalent to about two thirds of South Africa's annual gold mine production.

The sale raised about US$3.8 billion which the Bank Nederlandsche said would be held in interest-bearing foreign currency reserves which would produce earnings of about 250 million guilders (US$140 million) in extra government revenue.
Silver remained relatively stronger than gold Thursday, with spot gold/silver ratio sliding to a four month low at 74.79, from 75.42 Wednesday.
COMEX March silver closed up 5.5 cents at $4.740 an ounce.
The April COMEX gold/NYMEX platinum spread slipped back Thrusday though to $7.30 an ounce, from a two month high at $9.00 on Tuesday.
NYMEX April platinum ended up $1.80 an ounce at $364.30.
Platinum mine output may rise around five percent in 1997 as South African operations return to normal after last year's labor unrest, Christian said.

But Russian shipments may decline slightly in 1997 and 1998. Meanwhile, platinum demand is running at a good pace, with Japanese auto production up for the first time in six years in 1996 at 10.3 million vehicles.
NYMEX March palladium closed up $1.75 at $124.50.
Russian palladium exports are expected to decline significantly over the next two years, perhaps by more than 10 pct annually, CPM Group said.
The demand outlook remains bright though, with personal computer sales worldwide up an estimated 19 pct in 1996.
Palladium paste is widely used in manufacturing semiconductors used in computers.
